title: Exercise signals: from contraction to PGC-1α
goal: Explain how the calcium, energy and stress signals of each session are sensed by CaMK, AMPK and p38 MAPK, converge on PGC-1α, and add up across sessions into lasting adaptation.

steps.title: Every session is a disturbance

claims.text: Exercise adaptations are driven by many signalling pathways linked to regulators of gene reading and protein making.

evidence.quote: Aerobic and resistance exercise represent extremes on the exercise continuum and elicit markedly different training responses that are mediated by a complex interplay between a myriad of signaling pathways coupled to downstream regulators of transcription and translation.

claims.text: Exercise is a challenge to homeostasis that triggers many integrated responses to the rise in muscle energy and oxygen demand.

evidence.quote: To meet this challenge, multiple integrated and often redundant responses operate to blunt the homeostatic threats generated by exercise-induced increases in muscle energy and oxygen demand.

steps.title: Three sensors, one target
steps.text:
Each disturbance has its own sensor:

| signal | sensor | tells the fibre |
|---|---|---|
| Ca²⁺ | [CaMK](g:camk) (and calcineurin) | how much and how long it contracted |
| AMP up, ATP down | [AMPK](g:ampk) | fuel is short |
| ROS, stress | [p38 MAPK](g:p38-mapk) | it is under strain |

The Ca²⁺ sensors switch on factors that bind the gene for [PGC-1α](g:pgc-1a) [[c:sig-ca]]. A shift from ATP towards AMP switches on AMPK [[c:sig-ampk]]. p38 MAPK responds to ROS [[c:sig-p38]], and in rat muscle, raising Ca²⁺ alone switched on p38 and then PGC-1α [[c:sig-wright]].

The pathways cross-talk, but they converge: on PGC-1α, which coordinates [mitochondrial biogenesis](g:mitochondrial-biogenesis) [[c:sig-converge]].

claims.text: Calcium-sensitive enzymes (calcineurin, CaMK) act on factors that bind the PGC-1α gene and induce it.

evidence.quote: In this context, CnA and CaMK activities converge on the cAMP-dependent binding protein (CREB) and activating transcription factor 2 (ATF2, also called CREB2), which are activated by phosphorylation and dephosphorylation of respective Ser/Thr sites, subsequently binding to the promoter of the PGC-1α gene PPARGC1A and inducing transcription of this coregulator protein, among others ( 474 ).

claims.text: A shift from ATP towards AMP activates AMPK.

evidence.quote: For example, a shift in the ATP-to-AMP ratio toward AMP leads to the activation of a signal transduction pathway centered on AMPK, which in turn phosphorylates downstream protein kinase substrates ( 552 , 553 ).

claims.text: MAPK pathways, including p38, are redox sensitive and activated by ROS.

evidence.quote: MAPK signaling pathways are redox sensitive, and an activation of JNK, p38 MAPK, and ERK is observed upon elevated levels of ROS and RNS ( 537 ).

claims.text: In rat muscle, raising Ca²⁺ increased PGC-1α and mitochondrial biogenesis through CaMK and p38 MAPK.

evidence.quote: We interpret these findings as evidence that p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase is downstream of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase in a signaling pathway by which increases in cytosolic calcium lead to increases in peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator-1alpha expression and mitochondrial biogenesis in muscle.

claims.text: Signalling pathways such as AMPK converge on PGC-1α to promote mitochondrial biogenesis.

evidence.quote: Moreover, both AMPK as well as mTOR converge on the activation of PGC-1α to promote mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism of energy substrates ( 474 , 521 , 554 ).

steps.title: PGC-1α in human muscle
steps.text:
PGC-1α doesn't build mitochondria itself. It is a co-activator: it helps switch on a whole set of genes at once, the ones for mitochondrial proteins.

Human biopsies show it answering a single session:

- 3 h of knee-extensor work in 7 men: PGC-1α [mRNA](g:mrna) rose **7–10-fold**, peaking within 2 h [[c:sig-pilegaard]].
- Four 30 s all-out cycle sprints in 6 men: AMPK and p38 MAPK were switched on, PGC-1α mRNA about **doubled** at 3 h, but PGC-1α *protein* had not changed yet [[c:sig-gibala]].

A caution: in mice bred without AMPK or PGC-1α, many training adaptations still happen [[c:sig-redundant]]. The network has back-ups; PGC-1α is a hub, not the only road.

claims.text: One bout of exercise raised PGC-1α transcription 10- to over 40-fold and mRNA 7- to 10-fold, peaking within 2 h.

evidence.quote: Exercise induced a marked transient increase (P < 0.05) in PGC-1alpha transcription (10- to > 40-fold) and mRNA content (7- to 10-fold), peaking within 2 h after exercise.

claims.text: Four 30 s sprints activated AMPK and p38 MAPK and doubled PGC-1α mRNA at 3 h, without changing PGC-1α protein.

evidence.quote: Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma coactivator-1alpha (PGC-1alpha) mRNA was increased approximately twofold above rest after 3 h of recovery (P <or= 0.05); however, PGC-1alpha protein content was unchanged.

claims.text: AMPK, mTOR and PGC-1α are dispensable for many training-induced adaptations in animal knockout models.

evidence.quote: For example, three of the most characterized factors with putative roles in contraction-induced remodeling (AMPK, mTOR, and PGC-1α) are dispensable for many training-induced adaptations.

steps.title: Spikes that add up
steps.text:
How does one session's message become a season's change? A study took biopsies through seven interval sessions over two weeks [[c:sig-perry]]:

| after | PGC-1α mRNA | PGC-1α protein |
|---|---|---|
| 4 h after session 1 | over 10-fold up | – |
| 24 h after session 1 | back to baseline | +23% |
| sessions 3–7 | smaller spikes each time | plateau at +30–40% |

The mRNA goes up and down like a saw-tooth; the protein climbs in steps and stays up. [Citrate synthase](g:citrate-synthase) activity rose by session 3.

That is the general pattern: each session's response is short-lived, and adaptation is those responses adding up to a new steady level [[c:sig-accumulate]].

claims.text: Across seven HIIT sessions, PGC-1α mRNA spiked over 10-fold 4 h after each early session and returned within 24 h, while PGC-1α protein rose and plateaued at +30–40%.

evidence.quote: PGC-1α mRNA was increased >10-fold 4 h after the 1st session and returned to control within 24 h. This 'saw-tooth' pattern continued until the 7th bout, with smaller increases after each bout. In contrast, PGC-1α protein was increased 24 h after the 1st bout (23%) and plateaued at +30-40% between the 3rd and 7th bout.

claims.text: Many training adaptations come from transient responses to single bouts that accumulate into new steady-state transcript and protein levels.

evidence.quote: Many of the transcriptional changes that underpin these adaptations are the transient effect of repeated bouts of acute exercise that accumulate over time and result in new steady-state transcript and protein levels ( 87 , 198 ), even though disparate outcomes for transcript and proteins can occur ( 452 ).
the training-induced increases in transcriptional and mitochondrial proteins appear to result from the cumulative effects of transient bursts in their mRNAs

steps.title: ROS: a signal worth keeping
steps.text:
ROS are often sold as pure damage, so antioxidant pills sound wise. But ROS are also one of the messages.

In a [randomised controlled trial](g:rct), 54 young adults trained for 11 weeks on vitamin C (1000 mg) and E (235 mg) daily or a [placebo](g:placebo). VO₂max rose about 8% in both groups, but the mitochondrial marker COX4 rose 59% with placebo and not at all with vitamins; PGC-1α did the same [[c:sig-paulsen]]. A trial in 39 young men found the vitamins blocked rises in PGC-1α and antioxidant enzymes [[c:sig-ristow]].

Not every trial agrees: in 21 young men, 12 weeks of vitamins C and E changed nothing measured [[c:sig-yfanti]]. No good evidence shows they help [[c:sig-no-gain]]. High doses: no gain, possible harm.

claims.text: Daily vitamin C and E during 11 weeks of endurance training blunted rises in mitochondrial markers (COX4, PGC-1α) without changing VO₂max gains.

evidence.quote: Daily vitamin C and E supplementation attenuated increases in markers of mitochondrial biogenesis following endurance training. However, no clear interactions were detected for improvements in VO2 max and running performance.

claims.text: Vitamins C and E blocked training-induced increases in PGC-1α expression and endogenous antioxidant enzymes in young men.

evidence.quote: This was paralleled by increased expression of ROS-sensitive transcriptional regulators of insulin sensitivity and ROS defense capacity, peroxisome-proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARgamma), and PPARgamma coactivators PGC1alpha and PGC1beta only in the absence of antioxidants (P < 0.001 for all).
Molecular mediators of endogenous ROS defense (superoxide dismutases 1 and 2; glutathione peroxidase) were also induced by exercise, and this effect too was blocked by antioxidant supplementation.

claims.text: In moderately trained young men, vitamins C and E during 12 weeks of cycling training did not change any measured adaptation, including VO₂max and citrate synthase.

evidence.quote: Also, glycogen concentration, citrate synthase, and beta-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase activity in the muscle were significantly higher in response to training (P < 0.01) in both groups. However, there were no differences between the two groups concerning any of the physiological and metabolic variables measured.

claims.text: Antioxidant blunting of training adaptation is not a universal finding, and there is no convincing evidence that antioxidant supplements enhance training adaptations.

evidence.quote: However, this is not a universal finding, potentially indicating that there is redundancy in the mechanisms controlling skeletal muscle adaptation to exercise, meaning that in some circumstances the negative impact of antioxidants on acute exercise response can be overcome by training.
Importantly there is no convincing evidence to suggest that antioxidant supplementation enhances exercise-training adaptions.

debate.question: Do high-dose vitamin C and E blunt endurance training adaptation?

sides.position: Yes: in two randomised trials they blocked rises in mitochondrial markers, PGC-1α and antioxidant enzymes.
Not reliably: another randomised trial found no effect on any measure, and reviews call the blunting not a universal finding.

points: A session disturbs the fibre (Ca²⁺, AMP, ROS, stretch); signalling pathways sense each change and alter gene expression.
CaMK senses calcium, AMPK senses low energy, p38 MAPK senses stress; they converge on PGC-1α, the hub of mitochondrial biogenesis.
PGC-1α mRNA spikes within hours of a session and is back by 24 h; the protein builds up step by step across sessions.
Adaptation is many short-lived responses adding up to a new steady level; the network has back-ups, so no single switch is essential.
ROS are part of the signal: high-dose vitamins C and E blunted mitochondrial adaptation in some trials, not all, and never helped.

variants.stem: According to the signalling view, what is a single hard training session, at the level of the muscle fibre?

options.text: A disturbance whose signals trigger rebuilding in the hours after
options.why: Right: the session sends the message; the adaptation is the fibre's response during recovery.

options.text: The moment new mitochondria are built
options.why: Building takes hours to weeks after the session; during it the fibre is busy contracting.

options.text: Damage that the body only repairs back to normal
options.why: Repair alone would leave you where you started; training works because the response overshoots what was there.

options.text: A drain of energy with no lasting effect
options.why: The disturbance is exactly what leaves a lasting effect, through the signals it sends.

variants.stem: Three hours into a long ride, a cyclist's leg muscles are running low on glycogen and ATP turnover struggles to keep up: AMP rises. Which sensor does this switch on most directly?

options.text: AMPK
options.why: Right: AMPK is the fuel gauge, switched on as the ATP-to-AMP ratio shifts towards AMP.

options.text: CaMK
options.why: CaMK tracks calcium from contractions, not the fuel state.

options.text: PGC-1α
options.why: PGC-1α is the target the sensors converge on, not the sensor of AMP itself.

options.text: Citrate synthase
options.why: Citrate synthase is a Krebs-cycle enzyme and a marker of mitochondrial content, not a signalling sensor.

variants.stem: Late in a marathon, a runner's muscle fibres can barely keep ATP up and AMP builds. Which sensor responds most directly to this?

options.text: AMPK
options.why: Right: a shift from ATP towards AMP switches on AMPK.

options.text: p38 MAPK
options.why: p38 MAPK mainly answers ROS and stress, not the ATP-to-AMP ratio.

options.text: PGC-1α
options.why: PGC-1α sits downstream, where the pathways converge; it doesn't sense AMP.

options.text: CaMK
options.why: CaMK responds to calcium released with each contraction, not to fuel.

options.text: Calcium released with each contraction
options.why: Right: Ca²⁺ floods out with every contraction, so CaMK tracks how much and how long the fibre works.

options.text: A fall in ATP and rise in AMP
options.why: That is AMPK's signal.

options.text: Reactive oxygen species
options.why: ROS mainly act through redox-sensitive pathways such as p38 MAPK.

options.text: Low blood glucose
options.why: No sensor in the table reads blood glucose directly; CaMK reads calcium.

variants.stem: What does PGC-1α do in a muscle fibre after training?

options.text: Helps switch on many genes for mitochondrial proteins at once
options.why: Right: it is a co-activator, a hub that coordinates mitochondrial biogenesis.

options.text: Burns fat inside the mitochondria
options.why: PGC-1α is a gene regulator; fat is burnt by beta-oxidation enzymes.

options.text: Senses calcium released by contraction
options.why: That is CaMK's job; PGC-1α sits downstream of the sensors.

options.text: Carries oxygen from capillaries to mitochondria
options.why: That is myoglobin's role, not PGC-1α's.

variants.stem: After four 30 s sprints, PGC-1α mRNA doubled at 3 h, but PGC-1α protein was unchanged. Best interpretation?

options.text: The gene was switched on; the protein lags and builds over repeated sessions
options.why: Right: mRNA is the recipe, protein follows later; one session starts the process.

options.text: Sprints don't trigger mitochondrial signalling
options.why: They did: AMPK and p38 MAPK were switched on and the mRNA doubled.

options.text: The mRNA rise was a measurement error, since protein didn't change
options.why: mRNA and protein have different time courses; a lag is expected, not a sign of error.

options.text: Short sprints build mitochondria faster than long rides
options.why: One session with no protein change can't show that; it shows only that signalling starts.

variants.stem: A study takes one biopsy from triathletes 24 h after a hard session and finds no rise in PGC-1α mRNA. What does that most likely mean?

options.text: The spike was probably missed: it peaks within hours
options.why: Right: the saw-tooth rise returns to baseline within 24 h, so timing decides what you see.

options.text: The session sent no signal to the muscle
options.why: A single late time point can't show that; the spike may have come and gone.

options.text: These athletes can no longer adapt
options.why: Trained muscle still responds; the biopsy was simply taken too late.

options.text: PGC-1α protein must also be unchanged
options.why: Protein rises later and stays up; it can be raised while mRNA is back to baseline.

variants.stem: A cycling study biopsies riders before and 24 h after a long interval session and finds PGC-1α mRNA unchanged. What does that most likely mean?

options.text: The mRNA spike was probably missed: it peaks within hours
options.why: Right: in human muscle PGC-1α mRNA spikes within a few hours and is back near baseline by 24 h.

options.text: Interval sessions don't switch on PGC-1α
options.why: Interval sessions do: the spike just doesn't last 24 h.

options.text: The riders were non-responders
options.why: One badly timed sample can't classify people as non-responders.

options.text: PGC-1α protein must have fallen
options.why: No: protein typically rises a day after and stays raised.

variants.stem: Across two weeks of interval sessions, how does PGC-1α protein typically behave?

options.text: It climbs in steps after each session and holds at a higher level
options.why: Right: +23% after one session, then a plateau at +30–40% by sessions 3–7.

options.text: It spikes and returns to baseline within a day after each session
options.why: That is the mRNA pattern; the protein stays up.

options.text: It only rises after about six weeks of training
options.why: It rose 24 h after the very first session.

options.text: It keeps rising in a straight line with every session
options.why: It plateaued between the 3rd and 7th sessions.

variants.stem: A runner starting a 12-week base block plans 1000 mg vitamin C plus vitamin E every day 'to limit the damage'. Best advice?

options.text: Skip the high doses: they may blunt the muscle's response to training
options.why: Right: in some trials they blocked rises in mitochondrial markers and antioxidant enzymes, and no trial shows they help adaptation. No gain, possible harm.

options.text: Good idea: less oxidative damage means faster adaptation
options.why: ROS are part of the signal; blocking them blunted mitochondrial markers.

options.text: Good idea: the trial showed bigger VO₂max gains with vitamins
options.why: VO₂max rose about 8% in both groups; vitamins gave no extra gain.

options.text: It makes no difference to the muscle either way
options.why: One trial found no difference, but two others found blunted mitochondrial markers; with no benefit shown, the risk isn't worth taking.

variants.stem: A triathlete wants to take high-dose vitamin C and E daily through a training camp to recover faster. Best advice?

options.text: Avoid the high doses during training blocks: they can blunt muscle adaptation
options.why: Right: ROS are part of the training signal, and in some trials high-dose vitamins blocked mitochondrial and antioxidant-enzyme rises; none shows a benefit.

options.text: Take them: ROS are only harmful
options.why: ROS also act as signals that trigger adaptation.

options.text: Take them: they raised VO₂max more than placebo
options.why: They didn't: VO₂max gains were the same in both groups.

options.text: Take them only on hard interval days, when ROS signal most
options.why: That would remove the signal exactly when it is strongest.

variants.stem: In the vitamin trial, VO₂max rose equally with vitamins and placebo, but mitochondrial markers rose only with placebo. What is the fairest conclusion?

options.text: The vitamins blunted muscle adaptation; whether that hurts performance is unclear
options.why: Right: a molecular effect was shown, but 11 weeks of tests detected no performance cost.

options.text: Antioxidants are proven to make athletes slower
options.why: Performance and VO₂max did not differ between groups, so slower is not shown.

options.text: Mitochondrial markers don't matter, since VO₂max was the same
options.why: VO₂max is set mostly by delivery; mitochondria matter for submaximal endurance, which wasn't the main test.

options.text: The trial is uninformative because it was randomised and blinded
options.why: Randomisation and blinding are strengths; the limit is what was measured, and for how long.
